submission.natural_language_explanation: Bimodal single-anchor copy head: at each token it either parks on a sink (the passage's first token or a period) and writes ~0, or locks (attention ~1.0) onto one earlier-or-current anchor token and copies it onward over the following function words (and, of, in, the, commas, '?'), so its strength is set by which token is anchored. It is strong (0.45-0.9 of max, highest in long passages) when the anchor is a physical substance or material, food, chemical, drug, body part or disease word (asbestos, nicotine, glucose, rice, wine, coal, copper, cough, tumor), a rare proper-name or brand fragment (Tor of BitTorrent, Guang, Hong, Saskatchewan) or a non-Latin-script piece (Korean, Arabic, Icelandic letters such as ð/Ö), moderate (0.3-0.45) on everyday concrete objects (car, bus, engine, river, dog), and stays at ~0 for whole clauses built only from pronouns, person and role nouns (man, king, teacher, doctor, friend, mother), abstract nouns (idea, story, love, answer), weekdays or spelled numbers, and in Cyrillic text and short code.

rival_explanations: Broader: the head anchors on any concrete or common noun subject and copies it forward, so person nouns and abstract subjects (e.g. 'the plan was late', 'the men ... by rail') are active as often as substance words.

Narrower/different: strength is driven by token rarity and orthographic salience (rare subwords, proper-name fragments, non-Latin glyphs) rather than semantic substance class, so frequent food or material words like rice, wine or coal would stay near floor while rare person names would fire.
